United States and World War I (1914-1921)

primary_sources: Punch (London), "The Child Who Wanted to Play by Himself," December 1, 1919

stimulus.source_note: Punch (London) cartoon, December 1, 1919 (public domain). Caption quoted from the cartoon itself.
stimulus.text: Cartoon from Punch (London), December 1, 1919, titled "The Child Who Wanted to Play by Himself." A tall man, President Wilson, leads a small child wearing a hat marked "U.S.A." toward a building with columns labeled "TEMPLE OF PEACE," where other children play. Wilson says, "Now come along and enjoy yourself with the other children. I promised that you'd be the life and soul of the party." The child pulls back against Wilson's hand.

source: original; stimulus describes the Punch (London) cartoon, December 1, 1919
stem: The cartoon's picture of the United States refusing the League best supports which conclusion about American foreign policy after World War I?

options.text: The United States withdrew from all world affairs and became fully isolated
options.misconception: The United States stayed active in world affairs in the 1920s, through disarmament talks and trade. Refusing the League was not the same as withdrawing from the world.

options.text: The Senate's rejection ended Wilson's presidency and the Democratic Party
options.misconception: Wilson finished his term in 1921, and the Democratic Party continued. The rejection was a defeat for Wilson, not an end to his presidency or his party.

options.text: Britain and France also refused to join the League of Nations
options.misconception: Britain and France joined the League; the League was created without the United States, Germany, and Russia. The refusal was American, not Allied.

options.text: The United States rejected a binding commitment while remaining engaged in world affairs

rationales.A: The United States stayed active in world affairs in the 1920s, through disarmament talks and trade. Refusing the League was not the same as withdrawing from the world.
rationales.B: Wilson finished his term in 1921, and the Democratic Party continued. The rejection was a defeat for Wilson, not an end to his presidency or his party.
rationales.C: Britain and France joined the League; the League was created without the United States, Germany, and Russia. The refusal was American, not Allied.
rationales.D: Background from the books: the Senate rejected the League, but that rejection did not mean a turn to isolationism. The United States kept playing an important role in world affairs during the 1920s.
rationales.general:
1. Name what the cartoon shows. The United States refuses the League while Wilson coaxes it to join.
2. Ask what the refusal was. A refusal to join one binding organization, not a refusal to deal with the world at all.
3. Check what followed. Background from the books: the United States stayed active in world affairs in the 1920s, including disarmament talks.
Remember: refusing one commitment is not the same as refusing all contact, so do not stretch a single no into a full withdrawal.
